<!-- data-checksum: f354a6da47f62ead35825a3d2b8ef6d9 -->

Sometimes there is only one group of patients, and the comparison is with a number that comes from **outside** your data: a target set by the hospital, a value published by a registry, a benchmark in a quality report. Is our group different from that number?

::: {.callout-note}
## 💡 How every section on this page works
Each section answers one question about one of the practice's datasets: the joint replacement cohort, its patient-reported outcomes, or (for the binomial test) the hip fracture data. Its first code block loads the packages and the data, so you can jump straight to the section you need. Run that section's blocks in order, top to bottom. The "hypothetical" values below are made up for teaching; they aren't real registry figures or targets.

To keep the code short, the joint replacement examples use every case, including both cases of patients who had both sides operated on (80 patients in the whole cohort; [page 2](../foundations/02-demographics.qmd#setup) counts them). In a real study, decide how to handle them ([page 3](../foundations/03-distributions.qmd#paired)) and say what you did.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## ⚠️ Watch out: the value must come from outside your data
Choose the hypothetical value **before** you look at your data, and say where it came from. A value picked after seeing the results ("our mean is 84; let's test against 90") makes the p-value meaningless. If the comparison value comes from another group of patients whose data you have, compare the two groups instead ([page 6](06-two-unpaired-groups.qmd)).
:::

## One-sample t test {#one-sample-t}

**The question:** The operating room books 90 minutes for every primary joint replacement. Is our average operative time different from 90 minutes?

### When to use it

- The outcome is a **measurement** (minutes, kg/m², points).
- It's **roughly normal**, or the sample is large (about 30 or more) and not badly skewed ([page 3](../foundations/03-distributions.qmd#robustness)).
- Each patient is counted once and patients are independent of each other.
- If the data are skewed, bounded or ordinal → the [Wilcoxon signed-rank test](#wilcoxon-signed-rank).

### What the test really does

The one-sample t test asks whether the sample mean is far from the hypothetical value, compared with how much a mean like this would wobble from one sample to the next.

1. Take the **difference** between the sample [mean](../glossary.qmd#mean){.term} and the hypothetical value.
2. Estimate the noise in the mean, its [standard error](../glossary.qmd#standard-error){.term}: the [standard deviation](../glossary.qmd#standard-deviation){.term} divided by √n.
3. Divide: **t = difference ÷ standard error**. A t of 0 means the mean is exactly the hypothetical value. A t beyond about ±2 means the difference is large compared with the noise.
4. Turn t into a [p-value](../glossary.qmd#p-value){.term}: the chance of a t at least this far from 0 if the true mean really were the hypothetical value.

Once the test has run, a box under "Read the output" rebuilds t by hand.

### Look at the data first

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(tidyverse)

cohort <- read_csv("data/cohort.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

ggplot(cohort, aes(op_time_min)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 90, linetype = "dashed") +   # the booked time
  labs(x = "Operative time, minutes", y = "Patients")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](05-one-group-vs-hypothetical_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


## Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import stats

cohort = pd.read_csv("data/cohort.csv")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3))
ax.hist(cohort["op_time_min"], bins=range(45, 145, 5))
ax.axvline(90, linestyle="--")                        # the booked time
ax.set_xlabel("Operative time, minutes")
ax.set_ylabel("Patients")
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](05-one-group-vs-hypothetical_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png)
:::
:::

:::

A roughly symmetric hump, centered a little to the left of the dashed line at 90 minutes.

### Run it

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
op_test <- t.test(cohort$op_time_min, mu = 90)   # mu = the hypothetical mean
op_test
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

	One Sample t-test

data:  cohort$op_time_min
t = -8.2265, df = 599, p-value = 1.204e-15
alternative hypothesis: true mean is not equal to 90
95 percent confidence interval:
 83.1622 85.7978
sample estimates:
mean of x 
    84.48 
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
sd(cohort$op_time_min)                           # the SD, for the Results sentence
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 16.43613
```


:::
:::


## Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
op_test = stats.ttest_1samp(cohort["op_time_min"], popmean=90)   # popmean = the hypothetical mean
print(op_test)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
TtestResult(statistic=np.float64(-8.226498476022671), pvalue=np.float64(1.2039160411565963e-15), df=np.int64(599))
```


:::

```{.python .cell-code}
print(cohort["op_time_min"].mean(), op_test.confidence_interval())
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
84.48 ConfidenceInterval(low=np.float64(83.162196800282), high=np.float64(85.797803199718))
```


:::

```{.python .cell-code}
print(cohort["op_time_min"].std())                               # the SD, for the Results sentence
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
16.436134303765563
```


:::
:::

:::





### Read the output

- **t = −8.23** (`statistic` in Python): the observed mean is 8.2 standard errors below 90. The sign says which side.
- **df = 599:** degrees of freedom, n − 1.
- **p < 0.001:** a mean this far from 90 would be very unlikely if the true average were 90 minutes. The output prints `1.204e-15`, which is [scientific notation](../glossary.qmd#scientific-notation){.term}: `e-15` means "move the decimal point 15 places to the left".
- **mean of x = 84.48** (the first number on Python's second line): our average operative time.
- **95% CI 83.2 to 85.8:** the CI for our **mean**, not for the difference from 90.
- **SD = 16.4 minutes** (the last line of output): not part of the test, but the Results sentence needs it.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔍 Under the hood: the t statistic by hand

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
time_difference <- mean(cohort$op_time_min) - 90      # step 1: the mean minus the hypothetical value
time_se <- sd(cohort$op_time_min) / sqrt(600)         # step 2: the standard error, SD ÷ √n (600 procedures)
c(difference = time_difference, standard_error = time_se)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
    difference standard_error 
    -5.5200000      0.6710024 
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
time_difference / time_se                             # step 3: divide
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] -8.226498
```


:::
:::


## Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
time_difference = cohort["op_time_min"].mean() - 90        # step 1: the mean minus the hypothetical value
time_se = cohort["op_time_min"].std() / 600 ** 0.5         # step 2: the standard error, SD ÷ √n (600 procedures)
print(time_difference, time_se)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
-5.519999999999996 0.6710023731346747
```


:::

```{.python .cell-code}
print(time_difference / time_se)                           # step 3: divide
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
-8.22649847602267
```


:::
:::

:::

The mean is 5.52 minutes below 90, and its standard error is 0.671 minutes: −5.52 ÷ 0.671 = −8.23, the t the test printed.
:::





### Effect size and 95% CI

The effect size is simply the difference from the hypothetical value: subtract 90 from the mean and from both ends of its CI.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
op_test$estimate - 90    # mean difference
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
mean of x 
    -5.52 
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
op_test$conf.int - 90    # its 95% CI
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] -6.837803 -4.202197
attr(,"conf.level")
[1] 0.95
```


:::
:::


## Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
print(cohort["op_time_min"].mean() - 90)                        # mean difference
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
-5.519999999999996
```


:::

```{.python .cell-code}
print(op_test.confidence_interval().low - 90, op_test.confidence_interval().high - 90)   # its 95% CI
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
-6.837803199717996 -4.202196800281996
```


:::
:::

:::





Operations took 5.5 minutes less than the booked 90 on average (95% CI 4.2 to 6.8 minutes less). Whether that matters is a scheduling question, not a statistical one: over a day of four joints, it adds up to 4 × 5.5 = 22 minutes.

### How to report it

> **Methods:** Mean operative time was compared with the 90 minutes booked per case using a one-sample t test.
>
> **Results:** Mean operative time was 84.5 minutes (SD 16.4); the booked time was 90 minutes (difference −5.5 minutes, 95% CI −6.8 to −4.2; p < 0.001).

::: {.callout-warning}
## ⚠️ Watch out: a published mean has its own uncertainty
A one-sample test treats the hypothetical value as exact. A registry mean is itself an estimate with a CI. If you're comparing your patients with a published series and its CI is wide, say so, and don't over-read a small difference.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## 🔀 R vs Python: what the CI is a CI for
Both R's `t.test(x, mu = 90)` and scipy's `ttest_1samp(x, popmean=90)` report the CI for the **mean** (83.2 to 85.8), not for the difference from 90. Subtract the hypothetical value yourself, as above.
:::

## Wilcoxon signed-rank test {#wilcoxon-signed-rank}

**The question:** Suppose our practice's target is a 1-year KOOS JR of 80 points after knee replacement. Is our typical patient's score different from 80?

### When to use it

- The outcome is **skewed** or has a **ceiling or floor**, so a mean isn't a fair summary ([page 3](../foundations/03-distributions.qmd#transform)).
- It ranks how far each patient is above or below the hypothetical value. It doesn't assume a normal distribution, but it does need distances that can be compared, so the outcome must be a measurement.
- For an **ordinal** scale (satisfaction from 1 to 5), count the patients above and below the value and compare the two counts with a [binomial test](#binomial-test). This is called the **sign test**.
- Strictly, it tests the **pseudomedian** (the Hodges-Lehmann estimate below), which equals the median only for a symmetric distribution. With a ceiling the two differ a little; report both.
- If the data are roughly normal → the [one-sample t test](#one-sample-t) is more familiar and slightly more powerful.

### What the test really does

The Wilcoxon signed-rank test compares the scores with the hypothetical value by rank, so a few extreme scores can't dominate.

1. For each patient, take the distance between their score and the hypothetical value, and note whether the score is above or below it.
2. Set aside any patient who scores exactly the hypothetical value.
3. Line the distances up by size, ignoring the direction, and give each its position: its [rank](../glossary.qmd#rank){.term}. The smallest distance gets rank 1; tied distances share the average of their ranks.
4. Add up the ranks of the patients above the value, and separately the ranks of those below. Either sum can serve as the [test statistic](../glossary.qmd#test-statistic){.term}.
5. If the typical patient scored exactly the hypothetical value, the two sums would be about equal. The more one-sided they are, the smaller the [p-value](../glossary.qmd#p-value){.term}.

Once the test has run, a box under "Read the output" adds up the ranks by hand.

### Look at the data first

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(tidyverse)

proms <- read_csv("data/proms_long.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
koos_1yr <- proms |>
  filter(instrument == "KOOS JR", visit == "1yr", !is.na(prom_score)) |>
  pull(prom_score)

length(koos_1yr)       # how many patients
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 260
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
sum(koos_1yr > 80)     # how many scored above the target
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 170
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
sum(koos_1yr < 80)     # how many scored below it
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 90
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(tibble(score = koos_1yr), aes(score)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2.5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 80, linetype = "dashed") +   # the target
  labs(x = "KOOS JR at 1 year (100 = best)", y = "Patients")
```

## Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import pingouin as pg
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import stats

proms = pd.read_csv("data/proms_long.csv")
koos_1yr = proms.loc[(proms["instrument"] == "KOOS JR") & (proms["visit"] == "1yr"),
                     "prom_score"].dropna()

print(len(koos_1yr))              # how many patients
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
260
```


:::

```{.python .cell-code}
print((koos_1yr > 80).sum())      # how many scored above the target
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
170
```


:::

```{.python .cell-code}
print((koos_1yr < 80).sum())      # how many scored below it
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
90
```


:::

```{.python .cell-code}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3))
ax.hist(koos_1yr, bins=np.arange(35, 102.5, 2.5))
ax.axvline(80, linestyle="--")                         # the target
ax.set_xlabel("KOOS JR at 1 year (100 = best)")
ax.set_ylabel("Patients")
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](05-one-group-vs-hypothetical_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-18-1.png)
:::
:::

:::

260 patients: 170 scored above 80 and 90 below. 170 + 90 = 260, so nobody scored exactly 80 and nobody is dropped from the test. A ceiling at 100 and a long tail to the left: the rank-based test is the safer choice.

### Run it

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
koos_test <- wilcox.test(koos_1yr, mu = 80,
                         exact = FALSE, correct = FALSE,   # see the R vs Python box
                         conf.int = TRUE)                  # adds the Hodges-Lehmann estimate and CI
koos_test
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

	Wilcoxon signed rank test

data:  koos_1yr
V = 22698, p-value = 2.293e-06
alternative hypothesis: true location is not equal to 80
95 percent confidence interval:
 82.74996 86.10002
sample estimates:
(pseudo)median 
      84.35003 
```


:::
:::


## Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
# pg.wilcoxon() runs scipy's test and adds the rank-biserial effect size
koos_test = pg.wilcoxon(koos_1yr - 80, method="approx", correction=False)   # see the R vs Python box
print(koos_test)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
            W_val alternative     p_val       RBC  CLES
Wilcoxon  11231.5   two-sided  0.000002  0.337961   NaN
```


:::
:::

:::





### Read the output

- **V = 22698** (R) or **W_val = 11231.5** (Python): the test statistic, a sum of ranks. The two programs report different sums (see the R vs Python box); the p-values are the same.
- **p < 0.001:** scores this far from 80 would be very unlikely if the typical patient really scored 80. R prints `2.293e-06`, that is 0.000002293; pingouin prints `0.000002`.
- **(pseudo)median 84.35, 95% CI 82.7 to 86.1** (R only): the Hodges-Lehmann estimate of the center of the scores, with its CI.
- **RBC = 0.34** (Python): the rank-biserial effect size, below.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔍 Under the hood: the rank sums by hand

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
distance <- koos_1yr - 80                    # step 1: each score's distance from the target of 80 (+ above, − below)
distance_rank <- rank(abs(distance))         # step 3: rank the distances by size, ignoring the direction
sum(distance_rank[distance > 0])             # step 4: the rank sum of the scores above 80 (R's V)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 22698.5
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
sum(distance_rank[distance < 0])             # ... and of the scores below 80 (Python's W_val)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 11231.5
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
260 * 261 / 2                                # the two sums always add up to n × (n + 1) ÷ 2
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 33930
```


:::
:::


## Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
distance = koos_1yr - 80                        # step 1: each score's distance from the target of 80 (+ above, − below)
distance_rank = distance.abs().rank()           # step 3: rank the distances by size, ignoring the direction
print(distance_rank[distance > 0].sum())        # step 4: the rank sum of the scores above 80 (R's V)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
22698.5
```


:::

```{.python .cell-code}
print(distance_rank[distance < 0].sum())        # ... and of the scores below 80 (Python's W_val)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
11231.5
```


:::

```{.python .cell-code}
print(260 * 261 / 2)                            # the two sums always add up to n × (n + 1) ÷ 2
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
33930.0
```


:::
:::

:::

The ranks of the 170 scores above 80 add up to 22698.5, R's V (printed as 22698), and those of the 90 scores below to 11231.5, Python's W_val. Together they make 33930, which is 260 × 261 ÷ 2. Nobody scored exactly 80, so step 2 sets nobody aside.
:::





### Effect size and 95% CI

Two effect sizes are useful here:

- The **Hodges-Lehmann estimate** (the pseudomedian): a center of the scores, in points. It's the median of all the averages of pairs of scores, so it's less affected by the ceiling than a mean.
- The **rank-biserial correlation (r)**: from −1 (every patient below 80) through 0 (balanced) to +1 (every patient above 80). As a rough guide, 0.1 is small, 0.3 moderate and 0.5 large. It is the rank sum above 80 minus the rank sum below, as a share of their total: (22,698.5 − 11,231.5) ÷ 33,930 = 0.34.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

```
74.700 85.750 93.925
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 82.74996 86.10002

[1] 0.95
```

```
r (rank biserial) |       95% CI
--------------------------------
0.34              | [0.21, 0.46]

- Deviation from a difference of 80.
```

## Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
print(np.quantile(koos_1yr, [0.25, 0.50, 0.75]))      # first quartile, median, third quartile
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[74.7   85.75  93.925]
```


:::

```{.python .cell-code}
# Hodges-Lehmann estimate: the median of the averages of every pair of scores
def hodges_lehmann(x):
    x = np.asarray(x)
    i, j = np.triu_indices(len(x))          # every pair, including each score with itself
    return np.median((x[i] + x[j]) / 2)

print(hodges_lehmann(koos_1yr))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
84.35
```


:::

```{.python .cell-code}
# scipy has no CI for it, so use a bootstrap: recompute it on 9999 resampled datasets
boot = stats.bootstrap((koos_1yr.to_numpy(),), hodges_lehmann, vectorized=False,
                       rng=np.random.default_rng(2026))
print(boot.confidence_interval)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
ConfidenceInterval(low=np.float64(82.69999999999999), high=np.float64(86.05))
```


:::

```{.python .cell-code}
print(koos_test["RBC"])                               # rank-biserial r
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
Wilcoxon    0.337961
Name: RBC, dtype: float64
```


:::
:::

:::





The typical 1-year score was about 4 points above the target (Hodges-Lehmann estimate 84.4), and the rank-biserial r of 0.34 is a moderate effect: 170 patients scored above 80 and 90 below, and those above tended to be further from it. The median is 85.75 (IQR 74.7 to 93.9, the first line of output), a little above the Hodges-Lehmann estimate, as expected with a ceiling. R's effectsize also prints a 95% CI for r, 0.21 to 0.46 (its footnote only restates the target of 80); pingouin gives r without a CI.

### How to report it

> **Methods:** Because 1-year KOOS JR scores showed a ceiling effect, they were compared with the 80-point target using a Wilcoxon signed-rank test, with the Hodges-Lehmann estimate and its 95% CI as the effect size.
>
> **Results:** The median 1-year KOOS JR was 85.8 points (IQR 74.7 to 93.9); the target was 80 points (Hodges-Lehmann estimate 84.4, 95% CI 82.7 to 86.1; rank-biserial r = 0.34; p < 0.001).

::: {.callout-warning}
## ⚠️ Watch out: two different "Wilcoxon" tests
The **Wilcoxon signed-rank test** (this one) compares one group with a value, or two **paired** measurements ([page 7](07-two-paired-groups.qmd#wilcoxon-signed-rank)). The **Wilcoxon rank-sum test** compares two **independent** groups; it's the same as the [Mann-Whitney test](06-two-unpaired-groups.qmd#mann-whitney). Always write the full name.

Also: patients who score **exactly** 80 carry no information about the direction and are dropped from the test.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## 🔀 R vs Python: Wilcoxon defaults
- **The statistic.** R reports V, the sum of the ranks of patients **above** 80 (22698.5, printed as 22698). scipy (and pingouin) report the **smaller** of the two sums (11231.5). The two sums always add up to n(n + 1)/2, here 260 × 261 / 2 = 33,930, so they carry the same information and give the same p-value.
- **Exact or approximate.** For small samples without ties, both programs compute an exact p-value; otherwise they use a normal approximation. R adds a **continuity correction** to the approximation by default; scipy doesn't. We set `exact = FALSE, correct = FALSE` in R and `method="approx", correction=False` in Python so they match.
- **The Hodges-Lehmann CI.** R computes it by inverting the test. scipy has no function for it, so the Python code uses a bootstrap, a different method, so the two CIs differ slightly (82.75 to 86.10 in R, 82.70 to 86.05 from the bootstrap).
:::

## Chi-square goodness-of-fit test {#chi-square-gof}

**The question:** Suppose a national registry reports that its patients are 10% ASA class 1, 55% class 2, 33% class 3 and 2% class 4. Is our mix of ASA classes the same?

### When to use it

- The outcome is **categorical** with two or more categories, and you have hypothetical proportions for every category.
- Each patient falls in exactly one category, and is counted once.
- The **expected count** in every category (total × hypothetical proportion) should be at least 5. Otherwise combine small categories, or with only two categories use the [binomial test](#binomial-test).

### What the test really does

The goodness-of-fit test compares the counts you observed with the counts the hypothetical proportions would predict.

1. Work out the [expected count](../glossary.qmd#expected-count){.term} for each category: the total number of patients × that category's hypothetical proportion.
2. For each category, take (observed − expected)² ÷ expected, then add up the results. The sum is the [test statistic](../glossary.qmd#test-statistic){.term}, **χ²**: 0 when the observed counts match the expected ones exactly, and larger the further apart they are.
3. Turn χ² into a [p-value](../glossary.qmd#p-value){.term} with the chi-square distribution. This step is an approximation, and a poor one when expected counts are small. That is where the "at least 5" rule comes from.

Once the test has run, a box under "Read the output" rebuilds χ² by hand.

### Look at the data first

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(tidyverse)

cohort <- read_csv("data/cohort.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
registry <- c(0.10, 0.55, 0.33, 0.02)                 # the hypothetical proportions, ASA 1 to 4

asa_counts <- table(cohort$asa)
tibble(asa = names(asa_counts), observed = as.vector(asa_counts),
       expected = sum(asa_counts) * registry)
```

### How to report it

> **Methods:** The distribution of ASA classes was compared with the registry's using a chi-square goodness-of-fit test.
>
> **Results:** ASA class 3 accounted for 41.0% of our patients (95% CI 37.1% to 45.0%) and 33% of the registry's, and ASA class 1 for 6.0% and 10% (χ² = 27.0, df = 3, p < 0.001).

## ⚠️ Watch out: counts, not percentages
The test needs the **counts** of patients in each category. Feeding it percentages ("6, 50, 41, 3") gives a wrong p-value, because the test's precision depends on how many patients there are.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## 🔀 R vs Python: proportions or counts
R's `chisq.test(counts, p = ...)` takes the hypothetical **proportions** (they must add up to 1). scipy's `chisquare(counts, f_exp=...)` takes the expected **counts** (they must add up to the observed total). Same test, different inputs.
:::

## Binomial test {#binomial-test}

**The question:** Suppose the target is that 90% of hip fracture patients are operated on within 48 hours of admission. Is our proportion different?

### When to use it

- The outcome is **yes/no**, and you're comparing one group's proportion with a hypothetical proportion.
- Each patient is counted once.
- The binomial test is **exact**: it works for any sample size, including small numbers of events. (The chi-square goodness-of-fit test with two categories is its large-sample approximation.)

### What the test really does

The binomial test works out exact probabilities, with no approximation.

1. Suppose the hypothetical proportion were true. The binomial distribution then gives the exact probability of every possible result: 0 patients with the outcome, 1 patient, 2 patients, and so on up to all of them.
2. Find the probability of the result you observed.
3. Add up the probabilities of all the results that are no more likely than yours, on either side of the expected number. That sum is the [p-value](../glossary.qmd#p-value){.term}.

Because it uses exact probabilities, the test works for any sample size. Once the test has run, a box under "Read the output" adds up the probabilities by hand.

### Read the output

- **number of successes = 1034, number of trials = 1200** (`k=1034, n=1200` in Python): 1,034 patients operated on within 48 hours ("successes" is just the software's word for the outcome you counted).
- **p < 0.001:** a proportion this far from 90% would be very unlikely if our true proportion were 90%. R prints `2.682e-05`, that is 0.00002682.
- **probability of success = 0.862** (`statistic` in Python): our proportion, 86.2%.
- **95% CI 0.841 to 0.881:** our true proportion is plausibly anywhere from 84.1% to 88.1%. This is the exact (Clopper-Pearson) interval.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔍 Under the hood: the exact p-value by hand

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
probabilities <- dbinom(0:1200, size = 1200, prob = 0.90)        # step 1: the probability of each possible result, from 0 to 1200, if the target of 90% were true
observed_probability <- dbinom(1034, size = 1200, prob = 0.90)   # step 2: the probability of the result we saw, 1034
sum(probabilities[probabilities <= observed_probability * (1 + 1e-7)])   # step 3: add up every result that is no more likely (the small factor guards against rounding)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 2.681613e-05
```


:::
:::


## Python


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
import numpy as np

probabilities = stats.binom.pmf(np.arange(1201), 1200, 0.90)     # step 1: the probability of each possible result, from 0 to 1200, if the target of 90% were true
observed_probability = stats.binom.pmf(1034, 1200, 0.90)         # step 2: the probability of the result we saw, 1034
print(probabilities[probabilities <= observed_probability * (1 + 1e-7)].sum())   # step 3: add up every result that is no more likely (the small factor guards against rounding)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
2.681612856420021e-05
```


:::
:::

:::

If 90% were the true proportion, 1,080 of the 1,200 patients would be expected. Seeing exactly 1,034 would be very unlikely, and so would every result further from 1,080 on either side. Their probabilities add up to 0.0000268, the p-value both programs printed (`2.682e-05`).
:::





### Effect size and 95% CI

The effect size is the difference from the target: 86.2% − 90% = −3.8 percentage points. Its 95% CI is the CI for our proportion minus 90%: −5.9 to −1.9 percentage points. It excludes 0, which matches the p-value below 0.05. In patients: at 90%, 1,080 of the 1,200 would have been operated on within 48 hours, 46 more than were.

### How to report it

> **Methods:** The proportion of patients operated on within 48 hours of admission was compared with the target of 90% using an exact binomial test. 95% CIs for proportions are exact (Clopper-Pearson).
>
> **Results:** Within 48 hours of admission, 1,034 of 1,200 patients (86.2%; 95% CI 84.1% to 88.1%) were operated on; the target was 90% (binomial test p < 0.001).

::: {.callout-warning}
## ⚠️ Watch out: decide one- or two-sided before you look
A target invites a one-sided question: are we *below* 90%? A one-sided test roughly halves the p-value, so choosing one after seeing which side of the target you landed on makes the p-value too small. Use a one-sided test only when the protocol named it before the data came in, and a result on the other side would genuinely change nothing. Otherwise report the two-sided test, as here.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## 🔀 R vs Python: exact CIs
R's `binom.test()` and scipy's `binomtest()` agree on the p-value. R prints the exact (Clopper-Pearson) CI automatically; in scipy, ask for it with `proportion_ci(method="exact")`. It's a little wider than the Wilson interval that [page 4](04-describe-one-group.qmd#proportion) uses, which for these 1,034 of 1,200 patients runs from 84.1% to 88.0% (the last line of output under "Run it"). Either is fine; say which you used.
:::
